description: Caching the result of a deterministic computation keyed by its inputs, so repeated calls with the same inputs return instantly without recomputing. Trades memory for time.
structural_signature: A pure function with bounded input space whose evaluation is expensive relative to the cost of looking up a cached result; same inputs always produce the same output; cache invalidation is unnecessary because results never go stale.
canonical_examples: Recursive Fibonacci with a memo table (O(2^n) → O(n))
HTTP response caching keyed by URL + headers
cross_domain_examples: Medical diagnostics: lookup tables for treatment decisions when patient signature matches a previously-analyzed case
Legal: brief libraries indexed by case features; retrieval substitutes for re-research
Manufacturing: jig fixtures preserve tooling setups so the same part doesn't need re-tooling
Education: spaced-repetition flashcards memoize prior cognitive work the learner has done
references: Michie, D. (1968). 'Memo' Functions and Machine Learning. Nature 218.
Cormen et al., Introduction to Algorithms, Ch. 15 (Dynamic Programming)

description: Defer computing a value until its result is actually needed. Composes naturally: large or even infinite intermediate structures can be expressed and traversed without ever fully materializing.
structural_signature: A composable description of a computation is decoupled from its execution; consumers pull only what they need; producers can describe arbitrarily large or unbounded structures cheaply.
cross_domain_examples: Just-in-time manufacturing: produce only what's pulled by demand, not what's pushed by capacity
Open-source release engineering: lazy compilation of release notes until the cut
Litigation discovery: produce only documents responsive to specific requests, not the entire data lake
references: Henderson & Morris (1976). A Lazy Evaluator. POPL.
Bird & Wadler, Introduction to Functional Programming

description: Express a complex system as a stack of layers, each providing a clean interface to the layer above and depending only on the layer below. Lets each layer evolve independently as long as its contract holds.
structural_signature: Concerns at different levels of abstraction can be separated; each layer's complexity is hidden behind an interface narrower than its implementation; layers depend downward only.
canonical_examples: Operating system kernel ↔ syscalls ↔ libc ↔ application
Database storage engines beneath SQL beneath ORM
GPU shading: hardware ↔ driver ↔ shader language ↔ engine
cross_domain_examples: Banking: settlement layer ↔ payment rails ↔ wallet interfaces; each can be swapped without touching the others
Construction: foundation ↔ structure ↔ envelope ↔ fit-out; trades work in their layer
Government: constitution ↔ statutes ↔ regulations ↔ guidance; each level hides the one below from the level above
Education curricula: standards ↔ courses ↔ lessons ↔ exercises
references: Dijkstra, E. (1968). The Structure of the THE Multiprogramming System. CACM 11.
Parnas (1972). On the Criteria to Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules

description: Connect a sequence of processing stages so that each stage signals upstream when it cannot keep up; producers slow down rather than overwhelming consumers. Avoids unbounded queueing and the catastrophic failures it produces.
structural_signature: A producer-consumer chain where upstream throughput exceeds downstream throughput at least sometimes; losing data is unacceptable; queues exist but must be bounded; the system must remain stable under load.
canonical_examples: Kafka consumer groups with controlled fetch rates
TCP flow control via window size
cross_domain_examples: Hospital triage: ER signals upstream (ambulances diverted) when capacity is exceeded — pipeline backpressure for bodies
Restaurant kitchens: 'on the fly' tickets vs. 'in the weeds' — expediter signals backpressure to the front
Aviation: ground-stop programs are FAA backpressure to the flight network
Customer support: queue length thresholds trigger upstream rate-limits on signups

description: Design operations so applying them N times has the same effect as applying them once. Critical when networks may retry, duplicate, or reorder messages: idempotence makes 'at-least-once' delivery functionally equivalent to 'exactly-once'.
structural_signature: An operation is invoked across an unreliable channel; retries are cheaper than tracking exactly-once delivery; the operation's semantic effect can be expressed as a state transition that repeats safely.
canonical_examples: Database UPSERT / ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
Stripe's Idempotency-Key header on payment intents
cross_domain_examples: Voting: design ballots so a re-submitted ballot replaces, doesn't add to, the prior one
Procurement: PO confirmations are idempotent — re-sending doesn't double-order
Pharmacy: refill requests with explicit Rx number and date are idempotent against the prescription
Tax filing: amended returns supersede prior returns, not duplicate
references: Helland, P. (2012). Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition. CIDR.
Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture

description: Relax the requirement that all replicas of data agree at every moment; instead guarantee that, absent new updates, replicas converge to the same state eventually. Buys availability and partition-tolerance at the cost of read-your-writes invariants.
structural_signature: A system where availability and partition tolerance matter more than instantaneous global agreement; users tolerate stale reads in exchange for the system staying up; convergence (not immediacy) is the consistency contract.
canonical_examples: Email with eventual delivery via SMTP relays
cross_domain_examples: Land registries with regional offices: changes propagate, queries may be stale during propagation
Inventory across retail stores: per-store counts converge through nightly reconciliation
Medical records across providers: HIE eventual consistency rather than real-time global view
Standards bodies: drafts propagate through committees and converge on a published version
references: Brewer, E. (2000). Towards Robust Distributed Systems (CAP theorem keynote)
Bailis & Ghodsi (2013). Eventual Consistency Today: Limitations, Extensions, and Beyond

description: Optimize for novelty (distance from previously-seen behaviors) rather than for an objective function. Counterintuitively, this often beats objective-based search on hard problems where the objective lies behind a deceptive fitness landscape.
structural_signature: A search problem where direct progress toward the objective is deceptive (intermediate steps look bad even when on the right track); the space of behaviors is large but bounded; novelty can be measured (e.g. behavioral distance).
canonical_examples: Lehman & Stanley's biped-walking and maze experiments
POET (paired open-ended trailblazer): co-evolving environments and agents
cross_domain_examples: VC portfolio construction: fund the unfundable to find the things consensus misses
Drug discovery: combinatorial libraries explore chemical-space novelty rather than optimizing one scaffold
Editorial: assigning reporters to under-covered beats rather than chasing the news cycle
Hiring: deliberately interview candidates outside the typical profile to discover signals the screening rubric misses
references: Lehman & Stanley (2011). Abandoning Objectives: Evolution Through the Search for Novelty Alone. Evolutionary Computation 19(2).
Stanley & Lehman (2015). Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned (book)

description: Address data by a hash of its contents rather than by an externally-assigned identifier. Identical content has identical address; deduplication is automatic; integrity is verifiable; references are immutable.
structural_signature: A system where data identity is defined by content rather than location; integrity verification is needed; deduplication is valuable; references should not break when storage layout changes.
canonical_examples: Git's object database (commits, trees, blobs all hash-addressed)
cross_domain_examples: Academic publishing: DOI-by-content (rather than journal-issue-page) would auto-dedupe and preserve integrity through reformatting
Legal evidence chain-of-custody: hash-addressing exhibits eliminates 'is this the original' disputes
Visual art provenance: NFTs are content-addressed art records, well or poorly executed
Scientific data sharing: dataset-by-content-hash makes reproducibility a property of the address
references: Merkle, R. (1979). Secrecy, authentication and public key systems (Stanford PhD thesis)
